intro_html:
Neither of Hawaii’s 2026 plug-in bills passed, and the next chance is the session that opens in January 2027. Until then Hawaiian Electric’s rules apply in Honolulu: new customer systems, including those in its Smart Renewable Energy Non-Export program for systems that send nothing to the grid, apply through its Customer Interconnection Tool, and every Non-Export participant needs an advanced meter.

Hawaii’s solar-rights law, HRS §196-7, stops covenants, bylaws and even leases from preventing a solar device “on any single-family residential dwelling or townhouse that the person owns”, and defines the device by reference to those buildings. It does not reach an apartment in a Honolulu condominium tower, and it protects owners, not tenants.

Latitude matters here as much as law. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs, after the railing loss, give a vertical south-facing panel in Honolulu 510 kWh a year, the lowest of any state’s largest city, because the sun stands high for most of the year; east- and west-facing railings do slightly better, and the same panel tilted to 35° would make about 1,170 kWh. What still makes the numbers work is price: Hawaii’s 42.8¢ average is the highest in the country, and Hawaiian Electric’s own figure for Oahu homes in 2025 was 40.5¢.

faq: Does Hawaii's solar rights law cover condo apartments?

No. HRS §196-7 stops covenants, bylaws and leases from preventing a solar energy device on a single-family dwelling or townhouse the person owns, and defines the device by reference to those buildings. It does not reach an apartment in a condominium tower.
Which way should a balcony panel face in Honolulu?

Tilt matters more than direction. In balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for Honolulu, after the railing loss, a vertical 800 W panel makes about 510 kWh a year facing south, 543 facing east, 536 facing west and 576 facing southwest, while the same panel tilted to 35° toward the south makes about 1,170 kWh, because at Honolulu’s latitude the sun is high in the sky for most of the year.
